verses.verse:
लंघो निर्वर्तो बार्धक्यं पक्षैक परिपक्वता।
राग वाचक पुष्टिश्च गमकाश्च विविधास्मृताः।१०८।
verses.text: Laṅgha (skipping), nivarta (turning back), bārdhakya (gradual expansion), pakṣaika-paripakvatā (strengthening one side), rāga-vācaka-puṣṭi (reinforcing the rāga's identifying phrase), and gamakas (ornamental oscillations), held to be of various kinds;

verses.verse:
अन्यारम्भः समाप्तिश्च लयानाम् मिश्रणं तथा।
वक्रताऽ वृत्तयश्चैते गुणा स्त्वेकादशस्मृताः।१०९।
verses.text: anyārambha (beginning on a different note), samāpti (ending [on a different note]), likewise the mixing of layas (tempos), vakratā (crooked movement) and āvṛttis (repetitions): these are held to be the eleven qualities.

commentary.text: That is, from a practical point of view there are eleven main qualities used in tānas (fast melodic runs). And by mixing any two or three of these, many more qualities can arise; all of them are tāna-tattvas (elements of tāna). These qualities are described below with examples.

following.text: 1 - Laṅghana (skipping)
Laṅghana (skipping) is used in ascent or descent in two ways. One is on its own, as in (Sa Ga Re Ma Ga Pa); the other mixed with alaṅghana (not skipping), as in (SaRe SaGa ReGa ReMa)
2 - Nivartana (turning back)

The literal meaning of nivartana is 'returning'. When, before the ascent is completed, some part of the descent is mixed in and then the ascent is made again, this action is called nivartana (turning back). For example (Sa Re Ga Re Sa Re Ga Ga)
3 - (Bārdhakya) Baṛhat (gradual expansion)

In this action too nivartana (turning back) is necessary, but in it one has to return again and again to a fixed place and then advance regularly one note at a time; so it has an existence somewhat different from nivartana. For example - (Sa Re Sa, Sa Re Ga Re Sa, Sa Re Ga Ma Ga Re Sa, Sa Re GaMa Ma Pa Ma Ga Re Sa). In this way the group of notes keeps growing, step after step.
4 - Pakṣaika paripakvatā (strengthening one side)

It means strengthening one of the two sides, ascent or descent, in many ways. It is a more suitable action mostly for rāgas of the auḍava-sampūrṇa jāti (five notes in ascent, all seven in descent), as in Bihāg - ( Ga Re Sa, Ma Ga Re Sa, Pa Ma′ Ga Ma Ga Re Sa, Ni Dha Pa Ma Ga Re Sa)
5 - Rāga-vācaka puṣṭi (reinforcing the rāga's identifying phrase)

That is, presenting the group of notes by which the rāga becomes clearer, beginning it from different notes. This action is mostly used in saṅkīrṇa (mixed) rāgas. For example - to keep Rāmkalī apart from Bhairav -- Ma′ Pa komal Dha komal Ni komal Dha Pa komal Re Ga Ma Pa Ma′ Pa komal Dha komal Ni komal Dha Pa, Ṡa Ni komal Dha! Pa Ma′ Pa komal Dha komal Ni komal Dha Pa Ma Pa Ga Ma Ga komal Re Sa. Or, in a song, bringing out any one of these four aspects, words, sargam, notes and tāla (metric cycle), is also an example of it.
6 - Gamaka

This is a celebrated action, whose description is given in other treatises too. My view does not differ from theirs. (svarasya kampo gamakaḥ) That is, the use of shaken notes is called gamaka (ornamental oscillation). Performers use various kinds of gamaka with their skill, which are impossible to write down; but the ordinary gamaka, in which the sparśa (touch) note predominates, is like this: ( Sa Re SaGa ReGa Re Sa Re Ga ReMa GaMa Ga Re Sa). If the sparśa note is taken out of this, it will become merely an example of ekāvṛtti (one-note repetition).
7 - Anyārambha (beginning on a different note)
Its meaning is to begin from one note after another and end on one [note], for example - (in Yaman - Ṇi Re Ga, ḌhaṆi Re Ga, Ma′ Ga Re Ga, Ni Dha Pa Ma′ Ga Re Ga)
8 - Anya samāpti (ending on a different note)
Beginning from one note and ending on other notes, changing each time. For example - in Yaman Ṇi Re Ga, Ṇi Re Ga Ma′ Pa, Ṇi Re Ma′ Dha Ni, Ni Dha Pa Ma′ Ga Re Sa).
9 - Layānām miśraṇam (mixing tempos)

When a tāna (fast melodic run) is flowing in one laya (tempo) and suddenly, leaving that laya, its double or half laya is mixed in momentarily, again and again, we may call this action miśralaya (mixed tempo). Only accomplished sādhakas (practitioners) can do this. In it, the blending of many layas is more interesting, as, in Rāga Yaman itself - Ṇi ReRe Ga Ma′ - DhaPa Ma′ Ga Ma′ Ma′Dha -Dha Ni Dha NiNi Dha Pa - DhaDha Pa Ma′ Ga -- Ma′Ma′ Dha Ni Ṡa NiDha Pa Ma′Ga ReGa -Re Sa.
10 - Vakratā (crooked movement)

This action is useful for vakra (crooked) rāgas. For example GaRe MaGa PaMa′ DhaPa Ma′ Ga PaRe Sa, Ma′ Ga PaMa′ DhaPa NiDha Ṡa, and so on. 'In rāgas such as Gauṛ Sāraṅg - MaGa PaMa′ DhaPa Ma′Ga PaRe Sa. MaGa PaMa′ DhaPa NiDha Ṡa
11 - Āvṛtti (repetition)

It is mainly of three kinds, as in GaGa ReRe SaSa NiNiNi Re Re Re Ga. This we call ekāvṛtti (one-note repetition). And ṠaNiDha ṠaNiDha PaMa′Ga PaMa′Ga - this we call trayāvṛtti (three-note repetition). Repetition of more notes than this can indeed be done, but in practice it is not suitable from the point of view of beauty.

Besides the above 11 actions there are some more actions too, such as 'miśra saptaka' (mixed octave), that is, saying the same group of notes in two octaves, as in Ga Re Sa, Ġa Ṙe Ṡa. But for fear of enlarging the book, more actions are not being mentioned.
